sections.title: Core Foundations & Principles
sections.content:
• **Weight-Losing vs Pure Raw Materials**: Cotton is a pure raw material (weight doesn't change significantly during processing), allowing market-oriented or source-oriented localization.
• **Labor Intensity**: Being highly labor-intensive, it acts as a massive employment multiplier, especially for women in developing economies like India.
• **Backward and Forward Linkages**: Connects agriculture (cotton, jute, sericulture) with heavy engineering (looms), chemicals (dyes), and retail.

sections.title: Classification / Dimensions Matrix
rows: Oldest and largest organized sector; concentrated in Maharashtra and Gujarat due to historical black soil (Regur) advantage.
Prelims: Localization factors; Mains: Industrial stagnation in old hubs like Mumbai/Ahmedabad.
Concentric geographical concentration along the Hooghly basin in West Bengal due to water availability and monopoly on raw jute.
Prelims: Water transport role; Mains: Decline of sunset industry and diversification challenges.
Functional fabrics used in automotive, medical, agro-tech, and geotextiles.
Prelims: High-tech application; Mains: National Technical Textiles Mission and export diversification.

items.definition: Mega Integrated Textile Region and Apparel parks aimed at creating plug-and-play manufacturing hubs to reduce logistics costs and achieve economies of scale.
Accounts for the largest share of fabric production in India, characterized by small-scale units, lower capital investment, and fragmented operations.

items.title: Mnemonic: 4 Cs of Jute Localization
items.content:
• **Formula / Acronym**: C-C-C-W (Cheap Coal, Cheap Labor, Cheap Transport, Water).
• **How to Apply**: Instantly recall why the Hooghly basin became the prime jute hub.

upscNotes.content: Examiner Trap: Assuming cotton textile is strictly resource-tied to raw material sources today. Modern synthetic and powerloom sectors are largely market-oriented or agglomeration-driven.
Prelims / Mains Tip: Highlight 'Technical Textiles' and 'PM MITRA' as keywords for futuristic questions on manufacturing competitiveness and export growth.

keyTakeaways: The Indian textile sector is the second-largest employer after agriculture.
Geographical shift is visible from traditional centers (Mumbai/Ahmedabad) to decentralized clusters and eastern/southern states.
Government interventions focus on value addition, technical textiles, and global scale through parks.
